question: What is the most common histological type of uterine cancer?
explanation: Endometrial carcinoma originates in the inner lining of the uterus and makes up the vast majority of all uterine cancer cases. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h1)

question: Why does uterine cancer often have a favorable early-stage prognosis?

options.A: Symptoms like abnormal bleeding appear early, prompting timely investigation
options.B: Malignant cells in the endometrium are inherently slow-growing
options.C: The muscular wall prevents any metastasis until very late stages
options.D: Routine screening blood tests detect cellular changes before tumors form

explanation: Because the inner lining sheds or bleeds when disrupted by a tumor, women notice abnormal bleeding early and seek care before widespread spread occurs. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h1)

question: Which classification of endometrial cancer is typically estrogen-dependent and low-grade?
explanation: Type I endometrial cancers are common, estrogen-driven, and tend to have a less aggressive clinical course than Type II tumors. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h2)

question: What distinguishes uterine sarcomas from endometrial adenocarcinomas?

options.A: Sarcomas are strictly benign tumors that only rarely undergo malignant transformation
options.B: Sarcomas respond completely to oral hormonal replacement therapy
options.C: Sarcomas arise from the muscular wall or connective tissue rather than the glandular lining
options.D: Sarcomas are exclusively diagnosed in patients under the age of thirty

explanation: While adenocarcinomas originate in the epithelial lining of the uterus, sarcomas develop from the myometrium or stromal connective tissues. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h2)

question: The primary hormonal imbalance that increases endometrial cancer risk is prolonged exposure to unopposed:
explanation: Unopposed estrogen stimulates uninterrupted endometrial cell division, which is a primary driver for malignant transformation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h3)

question: A 60-year-old female presents with obesity, nulliparity, and type 2 diabetes. Which condition is she at highest risk of developing?
explanation: Obesity, nulliparity, and advancing age are classic risk factors specifically associated with endometrial cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h3)

question: What is the most common presenting symptom of uterine cancer?
explanation: Unexplained vaginal bleeding or spotting, particularly after menopause, is the primary clinical warning sign of endometrial malignancy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h4)

question: Why is any vaginal bleeding in a postmenopausal woman treated with high clinical suspicion?

options.A: Postmenopausal women cannot absorb iron adequately if bleeding occurs
options.B: Hormone replacement therapy guarantees total cessation of all mucosal shedding
options.C: Malignant cells completely destroy the vaginal walls within days
options.D: The endometrium should be atrophic after menopause, making bleeding abnormal

explanation: After menopause, estrogen levels drop and the uterine lining becomes thin and inactive, meaning any bleeding indicates pathological disruption. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h4)

question: Which diagnostic procedure provides definitive histological confirmation of uterine cancer?
explanation: A tissue sample obtained via biopsy or curettage is required to examine cellular architecture and confirm the diagnosis of cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a transvaginal ultrasound in a patient presenting with postmenopausal bleeding?

options.A: To evaluate liver function and rule out distant metastatic lesions
options.B: To measure endometrial thickness and determine the need for tissue biopsy
options.C: To remove small malignant polyps without invasive surgical procedures
options.D: To visualize cancer cells circulating within the pelvic lymphatics

explanation: Transvaginal ultrasound acts as a non-invasive screening tool; a thin endometrium rules out most cancers, while a thick stripe prompts a biopsy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h5)

question: What is the standard surgical treatment for early-stage uterine cancer?

options.A: Partial resection of the uterine fundus preserving the ovaries
options.B: Endometrial ablation and hormonal suppression therapy
options.C: Radical vulvectomy with superficial inguinal node dissection

explanation: Removal of the entire uterus along with the fallopian tubes and ovaries is the standard surgical management to eliminate the primary tumor and at-risk adnexa. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h6)

question: When is adjuvant radiation or chemotherapy typically recommended following surgery?

options.A: When the tumor is classified as a low-grade, early-stage Type I lesion
options.B: When pathology reveals high-risk features, deep myometrial invasion, or lymph node involvement
options.C: When the patient refuses surgical intervention due to personal preferences
options.D: When the patient desires future fertility preservation despite a malignant diagnosis

explanation: Adjuvant therapies are reserved for cases where pathological indicators suggest a higher likelihood of tumor recurrence or local spread. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h6)

question: What is a key postoperative priority following a total abdominal hysterectomy?

options.A: Encouraging heavy lifting to strengthen abdominal wall muscles
options.B: Restricting oral fluid intake for the first seventy-two hours
options.C: Applying continuous hot packs directly over the lower incision
options.D: Monitoring for hemorrhage and promoting early ambulation

explanation: Close observation for bleeding and early mobilization to prevent venous thromboembolism are critical components of immediate postoperative nursing care. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h7)

question: What information should be included when counseling a patient who has undergone a bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy?

options.A: Guidance on maintaining normal menstrual cycles using oral contraceptives
options.B: Instructions on how to perform daily self-catheterization for bladder spasms
options.C: Precautions regarding dietary restrictions to prevent permanent weight loss
options.D: Discussion regarding the onset of surgical menopause and symptom management

explanation: Removing the ovaries triggers abrupt estrogen withdrawal, leading to menopausal symptoms that patients must be prepared to manage. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h7)

question: What is the single most important prognostic factor in uterine cancer?

options.A: Body mass index prior to surgical intervention
options.B: Stage of the disease at the time of diagnosis
options.C: Presence of a family history of colon cancer
options.D: Patient age at initial symptom presentation

explanation: The extent of disease spread (staging) is the most critical determinant of overall survival and prognosis in uterine malignancies. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h8)

question: Which complication is commonly associated with pelvic lymph node dissection during uterine cancer surgery?
explanation: Disruption or removal of pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes impairs lymphatic drainage, frequently resulting in swelling of the legs. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h8)
